questions.q: Name the two main types of iron ore found in India and state the typical iron percentage range for each.
questions.a: Haematite (Fe₂O₃) — 60–70% iron; Magnetite (Fe₃O₄) — up to 72% iron. A wrong answer (e.g., naming limonite/siderite as main types, or swapping percentages) shows the student has not memorised the NCERT-specific classification and may confuse minor ores with the principal ones tested in board exams.

questions.q: Why are India's major iron-ore deposits concentrated in the Peninsular Plateau and not in the Himalayas or the Northern Plains?
questions.a: The Peninsular Plateau consists of ancient Precambrian crystalline rocks (Dharwar/Cuddapah systems) that host Banded Iron Formations (BIF) formed 2.5–3.5 billion years ago. The Himalayas are young fold mountains with sedimentary/metamorphic rocks lacking BIF, and the Northern Plains are recent alluvial deposits with no bedrock exposure. A wrong answer citing "high rainfall" or "volcanic activity" reveals confusion between mineral formation processes and surface processes.

questions.q: On an outline map of India, a student marks the **Ballari-Chitradurga-Chikkamagaluru-Tumakuru belt** only in Karnataka. Is this correct? Justify using the states covered by this belt.
questions.a: The marking is **incomplete**. The Ballari-Chitradurga-Chikkamagaluru-Tumakuru belt lies **entirely in Karnataka** — so marking only Karnataka is correct for this belt. However, if the student labelled it as crossing into Andhra Pradesh or Tamil Nadu, that would be wrong. A common error is confusing this belt with the **Maharashtra-Goa belt** (which spans two states). The student must memorise each belt's exact state extent.

questions.q: Compare the Odisha-Jharkhand belt and the Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur belt in terms of (a) dominant ore type, (b) key mining centres, and (c) geological formation.
questions.a: (a) Both are **haematite**-dominant. (b) Odisha-Jharkhand: Badampahar, Mayurbhanj, Keonjhar (Odisha); Noamundi, Gua (Jharkhand). Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur: Durg, Bastar (Chhattisgarh); Chandrapur (Maharashtra). (c) Both occur in **Banded Iron Formations (BIF)** of the **Dharwar Supergroup** (Precambrian). A wrong answer claiming magnetite dominance in Durg-Bastar or listing Bailadila (which is in Bastar but often confused) without distinguishing states shows poor map-memory and inability to compare spatially.

questions.q: "India exports high-grade haematite but imports coking coal for steel plants." Evaluate this statement in the context of resource distribution and industrial location.
questions.a: **Partially correct.** India has **large haematite reserves** (high-grade, low phosphorus) suitable for export, but **coking coal reserves are limited and high-ash**, forcing imports for blast furnaces. Steel plants (e.g., Jamshedpur, Bhilai, Rourkela) are located near iron-ore belts (Odisha-Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh) but still import coking coal. A student saying "India has no coal" is wrong — India has thermal coal; the shortage is specifically **coking coal**. This tests understanding of resource complementarity.

questions.q: Design a one-page map annotation for a Class 10 board exam answer showing the four iron-ore belts, two major mines per belt, and the dominant ore type (haematite/magnetite) using standard symbols.
questions.a: A good annotation includes: (1) Outline map with four shaded belts labelled; (2) Symbol key: ◆ = haematite mine, ■ = magnetite mine; (3) Mines: Odisha-Jharkhand — Badampahar◆, Noamundi◆; Durg-Bastar-Chandrapur — Bailadila◆, Dalli-Rajhara◆; Ballari-Chitradurga... — Kudremukh■ (magnetite), Donimalai◆; Maharashtra-Goa — Goa◆ (haematite). Poor answers miss the magnetite symbol for Kudremukh, omit a belt, or use no key — losing 1–2 marks in the 3-mark map question.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Iron ore is a naturally occurring solid material from which metallic iron can be extracted ______; in India, the two principal types are haematite (Fe₂O₃) containing 60–70% iron with a reddish streak and non-magnetic nature, and magnetite (Fe₃O₄) containing up to 72% iron with a black streak and strong magnetic properties.

Fill in the blank: Observe a rusty nail (reddish-brown) and a magnet sticking to a refrigerator — these everyday objects hint at the two faces of iron ore: ______ (like rust) and magnetite (magnetic).
What is Iron ore? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Iron ore is a naturally occurring solid material from which metallic iron can be extracted economically; in India, the two principal types are haematite (Fe₂O₃) containing 60–70% iron with a reddish streak and non-magnetic nature, and magnetite (Fe₃O₄) containing up to 72% iron with a black streak and strong magnetic properties.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Step ______: Compare haematite and magnetite on a table — iron %, colour, streak, magnetism.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Iron ore?
questions.a: Students believe magnetite is the main ore mined in India because its iron content (72%) is higher than haematite (60–70%).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can (1) distinguish haematite from magnetite using iron percentage, colour, streak, and magnetic behaviour; (2) locate and name the four major iron-ore belts on an outline map of India; and (3) explain why the Peninsular Plateau hosts these deposits by linking them to Banded Iron Formations (BIF) in Precambrian rocks.
